title: Rama answers Parashurama
hookLine: Rama strings the bow, spares the sage, and one arrow spends a lifetime of merit
carry: punya: merit is real, and it runs out
last: STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.

cards: The king has begged and been ignored. The whole wedding party stands frozen on the road, the brides in their carriages, the soldiers with their hands near their swords.
Every eye is on one young man, just married, who has been told to string a god's bow and then fight a warrior who has made kings tremble. You might expect a duel. Valmiki doesn't write one.
What Rama does next is quick and quiet, and it ends with nobody hurt.

teach.b: Rama speaks politely and firmly. But you've taken me for someone weak. Watch.
He takes the bow out of the sage's hands, strings it, and fits an arrow. Then the surprise. You're a brahmin, Rama says, and related to my teacher Vishvamitra, so I won't loose this at you.
But a drawn arrow can't go to waste. It will destroy one of two things: your power to move freely through the world, or the worlds of merit you've won by your austerities. You choose.
And the fire goes out of Parashurama. I gave the whole earth away to the sage Kashyapa, he says, and promised not to stay on it at night. Leave me my power to move.

teach.h: THE WORLDS HE WON ARE GONE.
teach.b: Rama looses the arrow, and those worlds are gone. Here's the Hindu idea underneath.

teach.h: PUNYA: MERIT, AND IT RUNS OUT.
teach.b: The word is punya, merit: the good that builds up from good deeds and austerity, and it can win a stay in heavenly worlds. But Hindu teaching says those worlds don't last.

In the Bhagavad Gita, people who enjoy heaven come back to this world when their merit is used up. Many teachers read this scene that way: merit can be spent in a moment. And then the old warrior does what matters more.

teach.h: HE WALKS AROUND RAMA AND BOWS.
teach.b: He names Rama the undying Lord, walks around him with respect, and leaves for the Mahendra mountain.
The first book closes gently: Rama and Sita at home, and Bharata gone to visit his mother's family far away. It matters very soon.

how: In devotional readings this episode is heard as one avatar of Vishnu meeting the next, and the Bala Kanda as the happy prelude before the Ayodhya Kanda's exile.

o: a battle Rama wins by shooting the sage down
a quarrel Dasharatha settles by giving up his crown
the dare Rama meets by stringing the bow and sparing him

games.q: the bow and the arrow — tap the pairs.
p: is given Vishnu's bow to keep

s: Rama kills Parashurama on the road
he spares him as a brahmin and takes only the worlds he had won.
before leaving he names him the undying Lord, slayer of Madhu.
heavenly worlds won by merit last forever
in the Gita, people come back to this world once their merit is used up.

games.q: you're Parashurama. one arrow will take either your freedom to roam the earth or the heavens your austerities earned. what do you give up?
o: the heavens; merit can be spent.
games.why: he gives up the worlds he'd won by austerity, then names Rama the undying Lord. Hindu texts teach that heavens won by merit end when the merit is spent.

practice: Parashurama walked around Rama with respect, the way Hindus circle a shrine with the holy on their right.
If you pray, stand and turn once slowly in place, clockwise, hands together, the way many families end their puja, and offer whatever good you did today without counting it.
If you don't pray, stand and turn slowly once anyway, and let one good thing you did today go without keeping score.

wordCard.voice: Parashurama's challenge, answered. Rama strings Vishnu's bow, spares the sage, and his arrow takes only the worlds of merit the sage had won.

orig.note: Sanskrit puṇya: merit, the good that builds up from good deeds and austerity. it can win heavenly worlds, and it can be spent.

carryVoice: Your line: punya, merit is real, and it runs out. Parashurama spent his heavens and bowed to the Lord. Day five hundred thirteen, and the first book is done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 76 (Rama strings the bow; Parashurama leaves)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 77 (return to Ayodhya; Bharata to Kekaya; Rama and Sita)
Bhagavad Gita 9.20–21 (heaven won by merit; return when merit is spent)
